tips.title: Je voudrais opens anything
tips.body: *Je voudrais un billet / une chambre / un café.* It is polite, it is the familiar conditional the specification explicitly allows, and it works in all ten settings. If a prompt says buy, order or book, start there.

tips.title: Count the questions before you start
tips.body: **One** at Foundation, **two** at Higher. Scan the five bullets and mark the ones with a question mark before the teacher begins — a missing question is a missing utterance, and it is the requirement most often forgotten.

tips.title: Est-ce que makes any question
tips.body: Put *est-ce que* in front of a statement and it becomes a question: *Est-ce que vous avez…?*, *Est-ce qu'il y a…?*, *Est-ce que c'est compris ?* One structure covers every question you need to ask.

tips.title: Je vais is enough for the future
tips.body: The Higher requirement is a **future timeframe**, not the simple future. *Je vais rester*, *je vais arriver*, *je vais visiter* all satisfy it. Decide in advance that any question about later gets a *je vais* answer.

tips.title: Communication only, so say something
tips.body: The task assesses **communication**, not accuracy. *C'est une sorte de…* scores where a silent search for the exact word scores nothing. And the formal register is **not required**, so do not spend thinking time on *tu* against *vous*.

why.matters: The role play is Task 2 of the speaking exam, worth 10 marks, and it is the most predictable part of the paper: a card with a setting, five prompts in English, a teacher who opens and asks the questions. The topic exists because the task is marked on communication only, so a reply that is understood scores and a silent search for the right ending does not; because every role play is transactional, getting something done in a shop, a hotel, a station; and because one prompt always says *ask*, which is a mark lost before you speak if you miss it.

Read the whole card before the teacher starts and count the questions you are asked to ask, one at Foundation and two at Higher, because the *ask* prompt is the one candidates skip. At Higher one reply must use a future, and *je vais* plus an infinitive is enough. Five bullets, five utterances, and the task is done.

steps.title: Ce que c'est
steps.body:
The **role play** is **Task 2** of the speaking exam and is worth **10 marks**.

You are given a **student card** with the **setting**, and **instructions and prompts in English**. The teacher has their own card with the exact questions. The teacher **opens the role play** with an introduction and then asks the first question.

Three things about it are worth knowing before anything else, because they change how you prepare.

**It assesses communication only.** The specification says so directly. You are marked on whether you get the message across — not on perfect grammar. A reply that is understood scores; a silent search for the right ending does not.

**Every role play is *transactional*.** That means getting something done: buying, booking, ordering, asking, complaining. It is not a conversation about your opinions on the environment.

**All role plays are set in a formal context — but you are *not required* to use the formal register.** So you will be in a shop or a hotel talking to a stranger, and *tu* will not be penalised. That surprises people, and it removes a worry worth removing.

The card is designed so you can answer using vocabulary from the **vocabulary list**. Nothing exotic is needed.

steps.title: Les dix contextes
steps.body:
The role play is **always** in one of **ten settings**, and the specification names them. Each exam series uses **six different settings** drawn from this list, so you cannot predict which — but you can prepare all ten, and there are only ten.

- **Café / restaurant**
- **Shop / market / shopping centre**
- **Hotel**
- **Train station**
- **Tourist information office**
- **Cinema / theatre / concert hall**
- **Campsite**
- **Leisure centre**
- **Doctor's surgery / hospital**
- **In town**

Notice how much they overlap. Almost all of them involve some combination of: asking what is available, asking the price or the time, saying what you want, and asking a question back. Prepare those four things and you are most of the way through **any** of the ten.

That is the useful way to revise this: not ten separate scripts, but **one set of phrases that works everywhere**, plus a handful of words specific to each place.

steps.title: Ce qu'il faut faire
steps.body:
Your card has **five bullet points**, and each one asks for **one utterance**. What differs between the tiers is the questions.

**Foundation tier**

- five bullet points, **five utterances**
- you must **ask one question**
- you speak in the **present tense**, or a familiar conditional where it is more natural — *je voudrais*

**Higher tier**

- five bullet points, **five utterances**
- you must **ask two questions**
- present tense or familiar conditional, as above
- you must **respond to one question asked using a future timeframe**

So the Higher tier adds **one more question to ask** and **one answer in a future timeframe**. Everything else is the same.

**The bullet point with a question mark is not optional.** If a bullet says *ask about the price*, an answer that describes what you want but never asks anything has missed a required utterance. Look through the five bullets before you start and mark which ones are questions.

**A future timeframe** need not be complicated. *Je vais rester deux nuits* — I am going to stay two nights — is a future timeframe using the near future, and that is enough. You do not need the simple future.

steps.title: Les huit types d'échange
steps.body:
The specification lists **eight** kinds of interaction a role play might ask for. Knowing the list means no prompt can surprise you — every bullet point will be one of these:

- **make transactions** — buying tickets, ordering food
- **make plans, appointments or reservations**
- **explain or give reasons**
- **describe**
- **express likes, dislikes, preferences or opinions**
- **ask for advice**
- **make a complaint or report a problem**
- **ask or talk about activities**

For each, one phrase is enough to start:

| The prompt asks you to | Start with |
|---|---|
| buy or order | *Je voudrais…* |
| book or arrange | *Je voudrais réserver…* |
| give a reason | *parce que…* |
| describe | *C'est…* / *Il y a…* |
| give an opinion | *J'aime…* / *Je préfère…* |
| ask for advice | *Qu'est-ce que vous recommandez ?* |
| complain | *…ne marche pas* / *Il y a un problème* |
| ask about activities | *Qu'est-ce qu'on peut faire ?* |

That table is the whole task, in eight lines. Learn the right-hand column and any prompt has an opening.

steps.title: À toi : trois jeux de rôle
steps.body:
**Jeu de rôle 1 — Au café.** Prompts: order a drink; order something to eat; say you do not want something; ask for the bill; ask one question.

**Jeu de rôle 2 — À la gare.** Prompts: buy a ticket to Paris; say single or return; ask the time of the next train; ask which platform; ask one more question.

**Jeu de rôle 3 — Chez le médecin.** Prompts: say what hurts; say how long for; ask for advice; say you cannot come on Tuesday; ask one question.

For each one:

1. Write your five utterances.
2. Mark which are **questions** — you need **one** at Foundation, **two** at Higher.
3. Check you could say each in **one breath**. If not, shorten it.
4. For Higher, prepare one answer in a **future timeframe**, using *je vais* + infinitive.

The most useful practice is saying them **aloud**. A sentence that reads well and cannot be said is worth nothing in a speaking exam.

steps.title: Aller plus loin : ce qui fait perdre des points
steps.body:
**Communication is what is marked — so say something.** The role play assesses **communication only**. A reply that is grammatically imperfect but understood scores; silence does not. If the right word will not come, say it another way: *je ne sais pas le mot, mais c'est pour dormir* communicates more than a pause.

**Answer the bullet you were given.** Each of the five bullets asks for its own utterance. A long, fluent answer to bullet 3 does not make up for skipping bullet 4. Five bullets, five replies.

**Count your questions before you start.** One at Foundation, **two at Higher**. It is the requirement most often missed, because a question feels like a small thing next to giving information — but a missing question is a missing utterance. Scan the five bullets first and mark the ones with a question mark.

**Higher: have a future ready.** You must respond to one question in a **future timeframe**. It needs nothing fancy — *je vais rester*, *je vais arriver*, *je vais visiter*. Decide before you go in that any question about later gets a *je vais* answer.

**Keep replies short.** These are transactions. *Une chambre double pour deux nuits* is a complete, correct answer; a subordinate clause is a chance to lose the thread. Short sentences also make the **one-breath test** easy to pass.

**The register worry is unnecessary.** Role plays are set in a **formal context**, but the specification says you are **not required to use the formal register**. Use *vous* if it comes naturally, but do not lose a mark's worth of time deciding.

**Prepare the phrase, not the script.** You cannot know which six of the ten settings will appear. What you can know is that nearly every one needs: *Je voudrais…*, *Est-ce que vous avez…?*, *C'est combien ?*, *À quelle heure…?*, and *Est-ce qu'il y a…?* Five phrases that cover most of ten settings is a far better use of revision than ten memorised dialogues.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- The role play is **Task 2** of the speaking exam, worth **10 marks**.
- Your card gives the **setting** and **prompts in English**; the **teacher opens** and asks the questions.
- It assesses **communication only** — being understood is what scores.
- Every role play is **transactional**: getting something done.
- There are **ten settings**, and **six** are used each series: café/restaurant, shop, hotel, train station, tourist information, cinema/theatre, campsite, leisure centre, doctor's/hospital, in town.
- **Five bullet points, five utterances**, at both tiers.
- **Foundation: ask one question. Higher: ask two.**
- **Higher only**: respond to one question using a **future timeframe** — *je vais* + infinitive is enough.
- Speak in the **present tense**, or a familiar conditional such as *je voudrais*.
- Role plays are set in a **formal context**, but the **formal register is not required**.
- The eight kinds of exchange: transactions, plans and reservations, reasons, describing, opinions, advice, complaints, activities.
- Learn **phrases that work everywhere** rather than ten separate scripts: *Je voudrais…*, *Est-ce que vous avez…?*, *C'est combien ?*, *À quelle heure…?*, *Est-ce qu'il y a…?*

questions.modelAnswer:
**The five replies.**

1. *Je voudrais un billet pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.*
2. *Un aller-retour, s'il vous plaît.*
3. *À quelle heure part le prochain train ?* — **question 1**
4. *C'est quel quai ?* — **question 2**
5. *Je vais arriver vers huit heures.* — **a future timeframe**

**Why this answer works.**

- **Five bullets, five replies** — each one answered, none skipped.
- **Two questions**, which is the Higher requirement. Mark the question bullets before you start so you cannot miss them.
- The last reply uses **je vais + infinitive**, which is a future timeframe. Nothing more elaborate is needed.
- Every sentence is short enough to say **in one breath**, and all the vocabulary comes from the list.

Notice what the answer does **not** do: no subordinate clauses, no reaching for impressive structures. The task assesses **communication**, and short clear sentences communicate.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would prepare for the role play task, and explain why preparing ten separate dialogues would be a poor use of time.
questions.solution: The specification lists ten possible settings for the role play, and each exam series uses six of them, so it is impossible to know in advance which setting will appear. Preparing ten separate dialogues and learning them by heart would therefore be a poor use of time, because at least four of them would never be used, and a memorised dialogue is of little help if the prompts on the card are not the ones that were rehearsed. A better approach is to learn a small number of phrases that work in almost every setting. Je voudrais is the safest way to ask for anything, est-ce que vous avez asks whether something is available, c'est combien asks the price, à quelle heure asks about times, and est-ce qu'il y a asks whether something exists. Between them these five phrases cover most of the transactions that any of the ten settings could involve, and only a handful of setting specific words then need to be added. I would also make sure I could ask two questions, since that is the Higher tier requirement and it is the thing most often forgotten, and I would prepare one answer using je vais plus an infinitive so that I had a future timeframe ready. Finally I would practise saying everything aloud, because a sentence that reads well but cannot be said fluently is worth nothing in a speaking exam.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Why not ten dialogues.** The specification lists **ten settings** and each series uses **six**, so the setting cannot be predicted — at least four dialogues would be wasted. Worse, a memorised dialogue helps little when the **prompts on the card** are not the ones you rehearsed.

**What to prepare instead.** A few phrases that work almost everywhere:

- *Je voudrais…* — asking for anything
- *Est-ce que vous avez…?* — is it available
- *C'est combien ?* — the price
- *À quelle heure…?* — times
- *Est-ce qu'il y a…?* — does it exist

Between them these cover most transactions in most of the ten settings, and only a handful of setting-specific words need adding.

**Then the two things people forget.**

- **Two questions** at Higher — the most commonly missed requirement.
- One answer with a **future timeframe**: *je vais* + infinitive, ready in advance.

**And practise aloud.** A sentence that reads well but cannot be said fluently is worth nothing in a speaking exam.

examTechnique.body:
Read all five bullets before the teacher begins, and mark which ones require a question.

Keep every reply short enough to say in one breath. These are transactions, not essays.

Start a request with je voudrais and a question with est-ce que. Between them they open almost every utterance the task needs.

At Higher, have one answer ready in a future timeframe, using je vais and an infinitive.

If a word will not come, describe it instead. Communication is what is assessed, and silence scores nothing.

Do not spend time deciding between tu and vous: the formal register is not required.
examinerErrors: Missing a bullet point, which loses a whole utterance.
Forgetting to ask the required questions, especially the second one at Higher.
At Higher, giving no answer in a future timeframe.
Stopping in silence while searching for a word.
Answering in long sentences that lose their way.
Using the perfect or imperfect tense where the present is required.
Worrying about the formal register, which is not required.
Reciting a memorised dialogue that does not match the prompts on the card.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats the role play as a transaction, not a performance: short replies, each one answering the bullet it was given. It checks the question bullets before starting, so the one-at-Foundation, two-at-Higher requirement is never missed, and it has a *je vais* answer ready for anything about later. It prepares phrases rather than scripts, because the setting cannot be predicted. And when a word will not come it says something else, knowing that the task assesses whether the message got across.
